claims.text: Adding approximately 2–3 at% Hf will promote formation of nanoscale Hf-derived oxide or intermetallic features.
The Hf-derived features will be evenly distributed throughout the alloy matrix.
Hf-derived oxide or intermetallic features will act as solute sinks.
The Hf addition will substantially suppress Cr-V-rich precipitate nucleation during irradiation up to 8 dpa at 300–600°C.
Suppressing Cr-V-rich precipitation will preserve the alloy's low hardening and radiation resistance.
The unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy can be produced by standard powder-metallurgy or casting methods with a uniform nanocrystalline microstructure.
Controlled oxygen levels can favor formation of nanoscale Hf oxides or intermetallic phases uniformly throughout the matrix.
Uniform Hf-derived features will inhibit local segregation of Cr and V.
The Hf-derived features will preferentially trap Cr and V atoms.
Trapping Cr and V will reduce their local concentrations and mobility.
Reduced Cr and V concentration and mobility will suppress nucleation and growth of Cr-V-rich precipitates during irradiation.
The Hf-modified alloy will have a significantly lower density of Cr-V-rich precipitates than the unmodified alloy.
The Hf-modified alloy will maintain low irradiation hardening.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain a uniform solute distribution with minimal precipitation after irradiation.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 begins forming Cr-V-rich precipitates near 8 dpa.
Cr-V-rich precipitation near 8 dpa in the unmodified alloy is accompanied by increased hardening.
The proposed effect is limited to doses up to 8 dpa and specimen temperatures of 300–600°C.
Processing can achieve a uniform minor-Hf distribution without producing deleterious Hf-rich phases.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes low hardening as a baseline property to be preserved, whereas the baseline field states that precipitation near 8 dpa is accompanied by increased hardening.
